newsitem.title: UK: Full text of July UK PMI services survey.
newsitem.headline: Full text of July UK PMI services survey.

text.p: Following is the full text of the July PMI Report on Services conducted by the Chartered Institute of Purchasing and Supply. The survey is sponsored by Reuters.
Skill shortages exert pressure on earnings and prices, but strong pound cools service sector growth slightly in July.

The service sector Business Activity Index continued to signal strong growth in July with one in three companies reporting expansion during the month. The index dipped for the second month in succession, however, signalling a slight moderation in the strong pace of growth seen in recent months.

Activity at panel member companies rose to meet a further sharp rise in the amount of new business placed during the month. Buoyant consumer confidence was again reported to have again played a key role in boosting demand, but the July survey saw the first evidence of the strength of the pound damaging the competitiveness of UK service providers, resulting in a slight slowing in the rate of growth of new business.
The rate at which new business was being placed nevertheless persisted at such a pace as to lead to a further increase in the amount of business outstanding at panel member companies.
In order to clear backlogs, and meet the current strength of demand, employment was again increased. One in five companies took on new permanent staff in July.

The sustained high level of demand for staff resulted in companies reporting continued skill shortages and often resulted in higher salaries. The growth of labour costs, combined with higher interest rates and higher fuel costs (resulting from the Budget), led to a further increase in average input prices and the first acceleration in the rate of input price inflation since April.

Rising input prices again encouraged firms to pass higher costs onto customers. Rates charges by service providers have now risen for nine successive months. However, as seen throughout this period, strong competitive pressures limited the scope for companies to pass on higher costs. Thus, whereas one in five companies saw their average input prices rise in July only one in ten were able to raise their charges.

A factor which has increasingly reduced the ability to charge more and thus maintain margins has been the strength of the pound. By raising the cost of UK services overseas (and reducing the cost of foreign services sold in the UK), the strengthened pound has forced increasing numbers of firms to cut charges, leading to the weakest growth in rates charged seen since last December.

Finally, firms generally remained optimistic about future growth in activity. Two thirds of the survey panel expect an increase over the next year. However, the strength of the pound and fears of higher interest rates caused the Expectations Index to drop to the lowest level recorded over the thirteen month history of this survey.
INCOMING NEW BUSINESS

Incoming new business rose strongly again in July. After seasonal adjustment nearly one in three companies reported an improvement on June levels, more than twice as many as reported a deterioration. The main driving force behind the increase in demand - as last month - was greater consumer confidence. However, the July survey found the first significant evidence of the strength of the pound leading to a loss of business. The rate of growth of incoming new business fell slightly for the second month running as a result.
OUTSTANDING BUSINESS

The amount of business outstanding at panel member companies rose again in July. The rise reflected the continued inability of companies to expand capacity at a sufficient pace to meet the rate at which new business has grown recently. A shortage of suitably qualified staff was again reported as a restriction on expansion. However, an increase in the number of companies that were able to clear backlogs led to a modest deceleration in the rate of growth of outstanding business. The rise in July was the smallest seen since January.
EMPLOYMENT

Employment again showed strong growth in July with all key sectors of the service economy reporting a rise in permanent staff levels. As seen in recent months, recruitment reflected the need to expand capacity to meet both actual and expected increases in business activity as well as the need to reduce backlogs of work yet to be completed. This survey has found service sector employment to have grown continually, and strongly, since July last year.
PRICES CHARGED

Average prices charged by service providers rose for the ninth successive month. The further strengthening of demand for services again allowed companies to pass higher costs on to customers while rising interest rates exerted additional upwards pressure. The rate of growth of charges declined to the slowest pace recorded since last December, however, as a growing number of companies reduced the rates charged for their services in order to compensate for the erosion of competitiveness caused by the strength of sterling.
INPUT PRICES

Input prices rose strongly again in July (and at a slightly faster rate of growth than in June). Three principal factors led to the increase: higher fuel costs resulting from the Budget, higher interest rates and, most significantly, further upwards pressure on wages caused largely by skill shortages. One in five companies saw costs rise on average, four times the number that saw costs fall.
(Where costs did fall it was usually attributed to the stronger pound reducing import prices.)
BUSINESS EXPECTATIONS

The Business Expectations Index continued to signal strong growth in activity over the next twelve months. Just over two thirds of all companies surveyed expected activity at their companies to rise over the next year while only 8% expected a deterioration. Although remaining very buoyant, the Index nevertheless slipped to the lowest level recorded over the thirteen month history of the survey due to a rise in the number of companies anticipating a downturn in business due to the strong pound and rising interest rates.
-- Richard Murphy, London Newsroom 44 171 542 2774
